title: SpaceX Starship Flies From Texas, Deploys 26 Starlink Satellites as Booster Splashes Down
excerpt: SpaceX launched Starship on its 15th test flight Friday from Starbase, Texas, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites, while the booster splashed down in the Gulf.
content:
SpaceX launched Starship on its 15th test flight Friday afternoon from Starbase, Texas, putting the upper stage into orbit for only the second time and deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites, while the Super Heavy booster was diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.

Flight 15 lifted off from Orbital Launch Pad 2 at Starbase at 4:47 p.m. CST on Friday, November 13. It is the fourth flight of the Starship V3 generation: Super Heavy Booster 22 and Ship 42, which SpaceX has nicknamed “Don’t Panic.”

Booster diverted, satellites deployed

The flight plan called for both stages to return to the launch tower to be caught by its arms — a first for the program. About six and a half minutes after liftoff, an unknown issue caused SpaceX to abort the Super Heavy booster catch, and the booster splashed down offshore in the Gulf, where it exploded as remaining propellant burned off. Three earlier boosters were caught by the tower, but a Version 3 Super Heavy has yet to make a successful return.

The upper stage fared better. Ship 42 entered low Earth orbit at about 275 kilometers and, starting about 35 minutes after launch, deployed all 26 Starlink V3 satellites over roughly 42 minutes. SpaceX confirmed all 26 satellites are in orbit and in contact. The batch adds about a terabit of data capacity to the Starlink constellation, roughly what 10 Falcon 9 launches of older satellites would carry.

A catch attempt still to come

As of Saturday morning, the mission was not over. Ship 42 is scheduled to circle Earth about 14 times over more than 22 hours, then attempt the program’s first-ever return of the upper stage to the launch site, with the tower arms catching it at Starbase at about 3:20 p.m. CST on Saturday, November 14. SpaceX said the ship and its heat shield are healthy, but the ship must still be cleared for reentry, the landing burn, and the tower approach.

This is the second Starship flight to deploy satellites into stable orbit. The flight could also be one of the last test flights from Texas before Starship operations shift toward Florida, where facilities at Kennedy Space Center Pad 39A are undergoing final testing.

What it means for Texas

Starbase, at Boca Chica in South Texas, is where the largest rocket ever flown is being tested and built. Each flight is a step toward SpaceX’s goal of a fully reusable rocket that can carry large payloads — and eventually people — to orbit, the Moon, and Mars. The V3 Starlink satellites deployed on this flight are designed to greatly expand the network’s capacity and user speeds, including for the rural and border communities across South Texas that rely on satellite internet. Webb Watch 956 will report the outcome of Saturday afternoon’s catch attempt.
